extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and readers interested in American poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for creating and assessing American poetry that is native, democratic, emotionally candid, and morally engaged; discusses desirable themes, style, and social role of poets in the late 19th-century United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free expression of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The poetry of the future aims at the free expression of emotion ... and to arouse and initiate, more than to define or finish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should prioritize candid, wide-ranging emotional expression that stimulates and begins processes in the reader rather than neatly concluding or fully defining ideas; emotional candor is central to modern poetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arouse and initiate rather than define
rubrics_metrics.description: "...to arouse and initiate, more than to define or finish."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective poems should suggest and provoke reader imagination and reflection (see Sainte-Beuve): leave things to be completed by the reader rather than exhaustively explaining every meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the reader / central identity (the Ego)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry has "direct or indirect reference continually to the reader, to you or me, to the central identity of everything, the mighty Ego."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verse should engage the individual reader's consciousness and sense of self, making the poem relevant to personal identity and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character over style or polish
rubrics_metrics.description: "Character, a feature far above style or polish ... gives predominant stamp to advancing poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive individuality and moral/psychological depth in poetry are more valuable than mere technical refinement or elegant surface; aim for expressive character rather than decorative finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Root poetry in outside life and landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be "more akin ... to outside life and landscape, ... real sun and gale, and woods and shores--to the elements themselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concrete, natural, and environmental imagery drawn from actual landscapes and lived experience over parlor-bound or purely literaryized descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fractional/select surface melody
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the prevailing flow: "an expression of mere surface melody, within narrow limits ... it is fractional and select. It shrinks with aversion from the sturdy, the universal, and the democratic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject poetry that is primarily ornamental, technically smooth, or designed only to please the ear; prefer sturdier, more universal work that can sustain democratic and broad human concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stimulate imagination and reflection (suggestiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The greatest poet is he who in his works most stimulates the reader's imagination and reflection ... The greatest poet is not he who has done the best; it is he who suggests the most."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry on its power to provoke thought and creative response; poems that invite interpretation and further thought rank highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: National / native American quality
rubrics_metrics.description: "A national poetry which was not English but American ..." and criticism that American poets "have caught the English tone and air and mood only too faithfully."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should develop an American diction, perspective, and principle of reproduction rather than merely imitating English models; seek original national voice reflective of American life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic subject-matter and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the highest walks of art it has not yet had a single representative worthy of it ... Never had real bard a task more fit ... to sing worthily the songs these States have already indicated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should represent democratic life and common people (farmers, mechanics, the native-born middle-class), treating national experience and mass material as worthy poetic subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage great national and historical themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems should treat "their origin, Washington, '76, the picturesqueness of old times, the war of 1812 ... the war of attempted secession of 1861-'65" and "the great problems of man and freedom."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage expansive treatment of national history and large civic themes (unity, liberty, civil war consequences) rather than stereotyped personal plots or trivial social topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's moral and prophetic role
rubrics_metrics.description: "To hold up high ... to dauntlessly confront greed, injustice, and all forms of ... wiliness and tyranny ... that is what first-class poets are for."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-class poets should act as moral voices confronting corruption and injustice; poetry should have the capacity to challenge social ills and inspire ethical responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate modern science and republicanism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Science, having extirpated the old stock-fables ... is clearing a field for verse ... Republicanism advances over the whole world. Liberty ... will one day be paramount ... Then only ... will the true poets appear."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry ought to absorb modern scientific understanding and republican ideals as foundations for new imaginative possibilities and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept importations but adapt humbly
rubrics_metrics.description: "Meantime, we can (perhaps) do no better than to saturate ourselves with, and continue to give imitations, yet awhile, of the esthetic models ... Let the sources be enlarged ... Remembering that at present, and doubtless long ahead, a certain humility would well become us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and draw from international literatures (British, Spanish, French, German, Scandinavian, Italian, Orient) but adapt and transform influences into a distinctly American expression with humility toward models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'beauty disease' (immoderate taste for beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fatal defects our American singers labor under are subordination of spirit, an absence of the concrete ... and in excess that modern esthetic contagion a queer friend of mine calls the _beauty disease_. 'The immoderate taste for beauty and art ... leads men into monstrous excesses.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid prioritizing beauty and decorative artifice above truth, justice, and moral balance; do not let aestheticism crowd out substantive poetic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor about sexual passion as legitimate poetic theme
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sexual passion in itself, while normal and unperverted, is inherently legitimate, creditable, not necessarily an improper theme for poet ... anything short of confronting that theme ... would beg the question."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sexuality openly and sanely in poetry and literature (in line with physiological and artistic honesty) rather than relegating it to euphemism, prudishness, or mere prurience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nude in art: legitimate when ethical and trained
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is necessary for the future of English art and of English morality that the right of the nude to a place in our galleries should be boldly asserted; it must, however, be the nude as represented by thoroughly trained artists, and with a pure and noble ethic purpose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual representations of the nude are defensible as artistic and moral education when executed by trained artists with noble ethical purpose; familiarity with ideal human form serves beneficial ends (e.g., counteracting harmful fashions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should foster international comradeship
rubrics_metrics.description: "I would inaugurate from America, for this purpose, new formulas--international poems ... the invisible root out of which the poetry deepest in, and dearest to, humanity grows, is Friendship."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for poems that reach beyond national borders to cultivate friendship and common humanity; promote universal themes that can contribute to global comradeship.
